newsitem.title: UK: INSIGHT - Hanson shares to head for 350p.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Hanson shares to head for 350p.

text.p: DAY'S RANGE * SUPPORT * RESTNCE* MA-25 * MA-200
+ Chart breakout by Hanson shares from 310p indicates a move up to 350p over the medium-term, technical analysts said.
+ The 350p target is a 50 percent retracement of the decline from 485p in 1994 to 220p in 1996.
+ Breakout from 310p completes a bullish inverse head-and-shoulders pattern and calculations from it also gives a target of 350p.
Shares in building materials group Hanson have broken above previous resistance at 310p indicating a run up to 350p over the medium-term, technical analysts said.

The stock bottomed-out from a low at 220p in November 1996 after peaking at around 485p in February 1994 -- prices being adjusted for the demerger of "old" Hanson's chemicals, energy and tobacco businesses.
"The mega downtrend from the start of 1994 will be broken with only a tiny move up (by the share price)," said Robin Griffiths technical analyst at HSBC James Capel.
Short-term market weakness may depress the stock a little, added Griffiths. "But a low above 300p would be a clear buy signal," he said. By 1125 GMT, the shares were up 5p to 316p.
The shares have already made the normal one-third retracement of that fall and ready to go on to make a 50 percent retracement which will take it to the 350p target.

A chart of Hanson shares shows an inverse head-and-shoulders pattern which began in March and may now have completed, analysts said. The pattern is unusual in that breakout would indicate a continuation of the uptrend from last November and not a reversal which is the more usual consequence.
The pattern consists of two shallow troughs which have neckline resistance at 310p either side of a more pronounced low at about 270p.
From chart theory the maximum depth of the pattern -- of 40p -- when added at the point of breakout at neckline resistance also indicates a move to 350p.
"Soon the market will not see it (the stock) as a dull one but a combination of the correct sectors fo current (market) conditions," said Griffiths.
